transaction_facts:
SUBJECT: Kenya Pipeline Company PLC, NSE ticker KPC, which static_data/listing_NSE.json carries under sector Industrial Services. KPC listed on the NSE on 9 March 2026 after an IPO in which the State sold 65 percent at KES 9.00 per share and retained 35 percent. The offer ran 19 January to 24 February 2026. Issued shares are 18.17bn and market capitalisation was reported at about KES 163.9bn.

WHAT CHANGED HANDS: on 19 October 2026 the NSE daily disclosure recorded one block trade of 4.5bn KPC shares, 24.76 percent of issued capital, valued at about KES 42.5bn (about USD 327m). Reported execution prices run from KES 9.02 to 9.36 per share. bne IntelliNews notes the implied KES 9.44 differs from the KES 9.02 close and that the exact block price was not independently confirmed.

WHO CONFIRMED: Aliko Dangote, at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London on 21 October 2026: "We bought 25 percent of their pipeline network for their distribution of petroleum products" (Bloomberg, carried by Reuters via CNBC Africa, and by Nation). He did not name the acquiring company. The Star reported on 22 October 2026 that the legal vehicle had not been publicly identified.

FROM WHOM: state-backed holders that had bought into the IPO. Nation (21 October 2026) and Daily Handle (22 October 2026) name the National Social Security Fund, the Public Servants Pension Scheme, the County Workers Pension Fund and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, with pension funds for Kenya Power, KPC and Kenya Ports Authority staff also in the offer; at least eight parastatals sold. Those parastatals held 38.35 percent after the IPO and their combined holding fell below 15 percent. The Star carried an unconfirmed claim that NSSF and Uganda's government were among holders of the acquiring vehicle; bne IntelliNews separately puts Uganda National Oil Company at 20.15 percent post IPO. The seller allocation is not publicly confirmed.

NAMED COUNTERPARTIES: the sell side was handled by Rock Investment Bank and the purchasing client was represented by KCB Capital, also called KCB Investment Bank, a KCB Group subsidiary (Capital FM, 20 October 2026; Business Daily via bne IntelliNews, 20 October 2026).

COMPLETION: the trade executed on the NSE block board, the buyer confirmed it publicly, and the President described the transfer as done on 20 October 2026. I found no CMA, NSE or KPC notice confirming settlement, registration of the transfer, a board seat, or any threshold declaration. energynews.pro reported in October 2026 that no public notification of a takeover threshold breach had been found. Board representation is described by Nation only as something the stake "could" bring, not as an agreed term.

WHAT IT GIVES ACCESS TO: KPC moves petrol, diesel and jet fuel from Mombasa to the interior and onward to Uganda, Rwanda, DR Congo and South Sudan over roughly 1,300 to 1,342 km of pipeline plus depots. Dangote said on 21 October that he plans a USD 1.5bn upgrade of the KPC network (Financial Times, via EconoTimes, 22 October 2026). No offtake, throughput or tariff agreement between Dangote and KPC has been reported.

SEPARATION FROM THE NIGERIAN REFINERY: this stake is not a refinery. Three separate things sit in the same news window. (1) Kenya Pipeline Company, a Kenyan pipeline and storage operator, listed on the NSE since March 2026, which is what Dangote bought into. (2) The Lamu project, Dangote East Africa Petroleum Refinery, ground broken 30 September 2026, valued at USD 16bn or KES 2.1 to 2.2trn, 700,000 barrels per day, commissioning targeted around 2030, nothing built or producing today. (3) The Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals (DPRP) IPO in Nigeria, opened to Kenyan investors through an inward unsponsored Global Depositary Receipt that is to list on the NSE. The CMA stated on 6 October 2026 that the IPO concerns the Nigerian refinery business and is not linked to the Lamu project (Swalanyeti, 6 October 2026). The KPC stake is a Kenyan midstream asset; the refinery that could feed it does not yet exist.
part_a_direct:
Three NSE-listed companies are named in a reported transaction or contract connected to Dangote's petroleum business, plus the exchange itself as venue. Only one of them is the asset he bought.

1. KPC, Kenya Pipeline Company PLC. DIRECT. The 24.76 percent block bought by Dangote on 19 October 2026 and confirmed on 21 October 2026. Sources: bne IntelliNews 20 October 2026; Reuters via CNBC Africa 21 October 2026; Nation 21 October 2026; The Star 22 October 2026. This is the only company whose own shares are the subject of a Dangote transaction.

2. KCB, KCB Group Plc. DIRECT, advisory only. KCB Capital, also called KCB Investment Bank, represented the purchasing client in the block trade (Capital FM 20 October 2026; Business Daily via bne IntelliNews 20 October 2026). The link is a mandate and a fee, not an equity or commodity exposure. Separately, National Bank of Kenya, a KCB Group subsidiary, is one of the approved custodians for the Dangote Nigeria IPO route (Swalanyeti 6 October 2026); I have no figure for either mandate.

3. SBIC, Stanbic Holdings Plc. DIRECT, contract. Stanbic Bank Kenya is the receiving bank and custodian for the Dangote Kenya GDR programme, holding the underlying Nigerian shares and handling FX conversion and dividend payment in shillings, with SBG Securities as investment bank (Stanbic note to the market, reported 1 to 2 October 2026; CMA approval of the short form prospectus 5 October 2026; Swalanyeti 6 October 2026). The relationship is a custody and placement mandate on the Nigerian refinery IPO, not a refinery offtake.

4. NSE, Nairobi Securities Exchange Limited. DIRECT as venue, unquantified. The block trade ran through the NSE block board, and the DPR GDRs are intended to list on the NSE. Both generate fee and levy income for the exchange. No reported figure exists for either, so this is a mechanism, not a measured link.

WHY THE OTHERS DO NOT QUALIFY: no NSE-listed company is reported as an offtaker of Dangote product, a contractor on the Lamu refinery, a shareholder in Dangote entities, or a counterparty to a fuel supply agreement. The Africa Report reported on 23 October 2026 that Kenya has not formalised a fuel supply agreement with Dangote and that officials are divided over whether he supplies the whole domestic market or only part of it. Kenya's other large marketers, Vivo Energy and Rubis, are not on the 65-name NSE list, so there is no listed retail counterparty even in principle. No jet fuel contract with Kenya Airways is reported. The honest summary is: one company directly as the asset acquired, two as paid intermediaries in the two Dangote capital markets transactions, and the rest is mechanism with no reported transaction.
mechanisms_by_sector:
Each entry states what changes in cost, volume or contract, and marks DIRECT or INDIRECT. No conclusion about share prices is drawn.

PETROLEUM LOGISTICS AND STORAGE. KPC is the entire listed sector. MECHANISM: KPC earns a regulated tariff per cubic metre per kilometre moved, so its revenue moves with throughput and with the EPRA approved tariff rather than with the price of the product. KPC, DIRECT: the tariff is KES 5.44 per cubic metre per kilometre, raised to KES 5.53 from 15 July 2026 and to KES 5.83 in July 2027 under the 2025/26 to 2027/28 control period (EPRA, via People Daily, 2026). Two conditions attach to any Dangote effect: Dangote's stated USD 1.5bn network upgrade would need EPRA to allow it into the regulated asset base and the tariff, and Lamu product would need a physical route into KPC's system, which does not exist. No other listed company operates pipelines, depots or tank farms on this list.

FUEL MARKETING AND RETAIL. Only TOTL, TotalEnergies Marketing Kenya Plc, is listed. MECHANISM: a marketer buys refined product at landed cost and sells at an EPRA capped pump price, so the landed cost change lands in inventory value, working capital and the import financing requirement, while the per litre margin is set by the regulator. TOTL, INDIRECT: it reported a 14.01 percent market share in the six months to December 2025, second behind unlisted Vivo Energy, and H1 2026 revenue of KES 84.42bn (Kenyan Wall Street, 30 August 2026); EPRA raised OMC margins by KES 5 per litre in 2025 (People Daily). No supply contract with Dangote is reported, and the market structure is open tender import, so a Lamu refinery would have to win share against imports rather than displace a contract.

AVIATION. MECHANISM: jet A-1 is a direct operating cost that is repriced at each uplift. KQ, Kenya Airways Limited, INDIRECT: total costs were KES 97.7bn in H1 2026 against a KES 16.08bn loss, and the CFO attributed the increase to fuel (Nairobi Business Monthly, 26 August 2026; 5050 Markets). The African Airlines Association said Dangote's entry into jet A-1 has provided some supply security on the continent and that East African expansion could help regional carriers (The EastAfrican). That is an industry body expectation, not a contract, and no NSE-listed carrier has a disclosed Dangote supply agreement.

POWER GENERATION. MECHANISM: liquid fuel is a cost of production only at thermal plants, and that cost is recovered through a pass-through charge rather than absorbed. KEGN, KenGen Plc, INDIRECT: it runs heavy fuel oil thermal capacity and tenders for HFO supply at Kipevu III (KenGen tender KGN-FUEL-001-2024). KPLC, Kenya Power, INDIRECT: the Fuel Cost Charge on every bill is the adjustment for fuel prices and the quantity of fuel burned, so KPLC collects it rather than carrying the commodity risk (Kenya Power bill components). UMME, Umeme Limited, NO EXPOSURE: Ugandan distribution fed by hydro, with no liquid fuel generation in the mechanism.

MANUFACTURING AND CEMENT. MECHANISM: refined product reaches factories as haulage fuel, standby generation and, for some boilers, HFO; in cement kilns the main fuel is coal or pet coke, not diesel, so the transmission is partial. BAMB, Bamburi Cement, INDIRECT: its 2025 annual report cites high energy costs, higher coal prices and logistics pressure, and 98 percent alternative fuel substitution at its Nairobi plant, which is the opposite direction of exposure to a refined product price. PORT, East African Portland Cement, INDIRECT on the same basis. EABL, BAT, UNGA, CRWN, CARB, BOC, FTGH, CABL, all INDIRECT through boiler fuel, captive power and inbound and outbound freight. None discloses a Dangote supply contract.

TRANSPORT AND HAULAGE. MECHANISM: diesel is a direct variable cost of moving freight, and pump prices are the transmission channel, with the Kenya Transporters Association linking fare changes to EPRA price reviews. XPRS, Express Kenya, INDIRECT: a logistics operator whose cost base includes fuel and subcontracted transport. CGEN, Car and General, INDIRECT and on the demand side only, because it distributes vehicles, equipment and generators rather than consuming fuel at scale. There is no long-haul road haulage operator on the 65-name list, so this sector has no clean listed proxy.

BANKS AND THE SHILLING. MECHANISM: petroleum is Kenya's largest single import line, so a change in the landed cost of refined product changes the foreign exchange requirement and the import financing need. The scale is documented: the 2025 import bill was KES 2.77trn, expenditure on fuel and lubricants was KES 583.7bn, about 21 percent of it, and the current account deficit was KES 373.3bn (KNBS Economic Survey 2026, via The Star, 30 April 2026). What I am not claiming: no NSE-listed bank discloses Dangote related exposure. ABSA, BKG, COOP, DTK, EQTY, FMLY, HFCB, IMH, KCB, NCBA, SBIC and SCBK have no reported transaction beyond the KCB and Stanbic mandates already listed, which are fee lines. The letter of credit channel to oil marketers exists in market structure, but I found no disclosure that quantifies any bank's exposure to it, so no company level shilling claim is made.

unverified:
1. Settlement and registration. The block trade printed on 19 Oct 2026 and the buyer confirmed it, but I found no NSE, CMA or KPC notice confirming that the transfer settled and was registered. Treat "completed" as completed at trade level, not as a confirmed registry change.
2. The acquiring entity. Neither Dangote nor any filing names the company that holds the shares. The Star reported this gap on 22 Oct 2026.
3. Sellers. Nation and Daily Handle name NSSF, the Public Servants Pension Scheme, the County Workers Pension Fund and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, plus staff pension funds. The Star's claim that NSSF and Uganda's government sit in the acquiring vehicle is explicitly unconfirmed in that report, and it conflicts with bne IntelliNews putting Uganda National Oil Company at 20.15 percent as a continuing holder. The per seller allocation is unknown.
4. Board representation. Nation says the stake "could" bring board seats and a say in strategic investment. No appointment, shareholder agreement or board seat has been reported.
5. Regulatory status. No CMA declaration of a takeover threshold breach, and no exemption notice, was found. The stake was structured at 24.76 percent, just under 25 percent, which multiple reports say avoided an approval process.
6. Size and price. Reported stake is 25 percent in Dangote's words and 24.76 percent in the NSE disclosure. Reported value is USD 327m in most reports and USD 335m in Business Insider Africa. Executed price is given as KES 9.02 to 9.36, and the implied KES 9.44 per share does not reconcile exactly with the rounded totals.
7. KPC IPO totals. Reported proceeds are KES 103.45bn (The Star), about KES 112bn raised against a KES 106bn target (Capital FM), and KES 112.37bn of subscriptions for KES 106.31bn of shares (bne IntelliNews). These cannot all be right and I could not resolve which is the settled figure.
8. No fuel supply agreement. The Africa Report (23 Oct 2026) says Kenya has not formalised one and officials disagree on exclusivity. Any statement that Dangote product is contracted into Kenya, or into any listed marketer, would be unsupported.
9. No Dangote contract with Kenya Airways, KenGen, Kenya Power, Bamburi, East African Portland or TotalEnergies was found. The aviation link rests on an AFRAA comment about supply security, which is an expectation, not a transaction.
10. Dangote's USD 1.5bn KPC network upgrade is a stated plan reported via the FT, with no timetable and no regulatory filing on how it would be funded or tariffed.
11. The Lamu refinery is a construction site. Ground was broken 30 Sept 2026 with commissioning targeted around 2030; no capacity, offtake or crude supply contract for it is verifiable today.
12. The KES 0.32 per share KPC dividend and the KES 1.44bn implied payout to Dangote's block appear in one report (Daily Handle) only and are not confirmed in a KPC notice I could read.
